articles.title: Twenty-five dead after fire on cargo ship in eastern China
articles.summary: Of the 42 people on board, 17 were were evacuated, CCTV reports.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Thick plumes of smoke rise from cargo ship fire in Qingdao, China By Phelan Chatterjee 
- Published 10 September 2026 
Twenty-five people have been killed in a fire on a foreign-flagged cargo ship docked at a port in eastern China, according to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV. 
Of the 42 people on board, 17 were were evacuated of which five are in hospital in stable condition, CCTV reports. 
The vessel was undergoing maintenance at a shipyard in the city of Qingdao when the blaze erupted at around 11:15 local time (03:15 GMT). It was put out just over three hours later, according to CCTV. 
Photos released by state media showed the vessel to be the Ocean Melody, a 190m (623ft) long Liberia-flagged carrier which arrived in Qingdao on 31 August, according to tracking site MarineTraffic. 
Image source, Xinhua Image caption, 
China's Premier Li Qiang urged the rescue of people trapped on board the ship 
Qingdao is a major trading hub and ranks among the world's busiest ports. 
It is unclear what caused the fire. An eyewitness told the AFP news agency there was thick smoke rising from the ship, but he heard no explosion. 
The country's leader Xi Jinping earlier called for "all-out" search and rescue efforts while Premier Li Qiang stressed the need to "prevent secondary disasters". 
The fire comes nearly a month after a shipyard explosion in the south-eastern Chinese province of Fujian killed a rescue worker and injured 12 others.

articles.title: Hong Kong's first leader after British handover dies
articles.summary: The tenure of Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong's first leader after Britain handed over the city to China, was marked by crises and protests.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Tung Chee-hwa was the first chief executive of Hong Kong following the 1997 handover By Kelly Ng 
- Published 9 September 2026 
Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong's first leader after the city returned to Chinese rule, has died at the age of 89. 
The former shipping scion took over the reins from the last British Governor Chris Patten in July 1997 when the UK handed Hong Kong back to China , ending more than 150 years of British control. 
Tung's rocky tenure was marked by the Asian Financial Crisis, two major epidemics, and historic protests which attracted criticism of his administration. He eventually resigned in 2005. 
Tung died on Tuesday night surrounded by loved ones, local media reported. His office described him as a man "devoted to his country and its people". 
Born in Shanghai in 1937, Tung graduated with a mechanical engineering degree from Liverpool University in the UK before moving to the US, where he worked at General Electric for almost a decade. 
In 1969, he moved to Hong Kong and worked in his father's shipping conglomerate, the Orient Overseas, eventually taking over the reins in 1979. 
His political career began in 1992 when he was appointed a member of Patten's executive council. 
Despite having little political experience, Tung was believed to be handpicked by Beijing to lead Hong Kong after the handover. He was seen as a loyalist, especially after China's state-run banks helped rescue his family business during a global slump in the mid-1980s. 
During a reception at the Great Hall of the People in January 1996, China's then-president Jiang Zemin walked across a packed room to shake Tung's hands – a widely photographed gesture that at the time famously signalled Beijing's backing of Tung for the top job. 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Tung Chee-hwa (right) took over from the last British governor Chris Patten in 1997 
The Asian Financial Crisis hit shortly after Tung took over, which sent home prices diving. His administration was also beset by a series of public health challenges, including a bird flu outbreak from 1997 to 2002 and the 2003 outbreak of Sars, also known as Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome. 
But Tung's biggest political challenge took place in July 2003 during his second term, when half a million Hongkongers took to the streets to protest against a proposed national security law they feared would threaten their civic rights. 
His administration abandoned the proposed legislation following the massive outcry, which also contributed to Tung stepping down in March 2005. 
At the time his declining health was cited as a reason - but some said he was pressured by Beijing to step down. 
Beijing ultimately imposed a national security law on Hong Kong in 2020, which authorities have argued is necessary to maintain stability. Critics however have called it "the end of Hong Kong" and say it has created a climate of fear in the city. 
Tung's last public outing was in July 2021, at an event marking the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Chinese Communist Party. He underwent heart surgery months later, according to reports. 
He is survived by his wife and three children. 
Hong Kong's former chief executives have paid tribute to Tung. Leung Chun-ying, who led the city between 2012 and 2017, described him as a "benevolent" leader who "won people over with reason". 
Carrie Lam, who was the chief executive from 2017 to 2022, said Tung's leadership made "a historic contribution with lasting benefits". 
China's state news agency Xinhua called Tung a "renowned patriot, distinguished social activist, close friend of the Communist Party of China". 
It also noted that Tung had served as one of many vice-chairmen of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, China's top political advisory body, for four consecutive terms.

articles.title: Trump shadow looms large over Brics as Modi hosts Putin and Xi in Delhi
articles.summary: As Brics leaders meet in Delhi, divisions within the bloc make a united response to Washington unlikely.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Chinese President Xi Jinping and India Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the Brics summit in Russia in 2024 By Vikas Pandey India editor, BBC News 
- Published 11 September 2026 
The US is not a member of Brics, yet President Donald Trump's shadow will loom large over the group's summit in Delhi this weekend. 
Leaders from 11 Brics nations - including host India, China, Russia, Brazil, South Africa, the UAE and Iran, with Saudi Arabia attending as an invited member - will hold talks on a wide range of issues. But few will be as consequential as the impact of President Trump's policies. 
The war in Iran and the ever-present threat of White House tariffs, directed at both US adversaries and allies, have destabilised global energy markets and has often left the global economy guessing the future. 
It is against this backdrop that Brics leaders are meeting. Yet the group is unlikely to produce a consensus statement that openly calls out the US or lays out a coordinated strategy to counter President Trump's policies and geopolitics. 
That is partly because Brics itself is deeply divided over how far it should go in challenging Washington. 
"India cannot afford to have a joint statement that rails against Washington," Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told the BBC. He expects any criticism of US policies to be "vague and indirect", reflecting the sharply divergent interests within the expanded group. 
While Russia and Iran may push for the group to take a clearer stand against President Trump, the geopolitical realities within Brics are likely to make that difficult. 
India, which is reportedly in the final stages of a trade deal with the US, will not want a statement that could upset the White House. China, too, may be wary of being seen as using Brics to target Washington. 
Then there is the UAE, which has come under Iranian attack during Tehran's retaliation against US and Israeli strikes. The Gulf state, which hosts US military bases, is unlikely to support a statement that helps Tehran's cause. 
Kugelman says Brics has become more significant through its expansion, but that has also made consensus harder. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
US President Donald Trump with India's Modi during a bilateral meeting at the G7 summit in France in 2026 
"You've added a number of members that don't get along," he said, describing the challenge for India as bringing together countries with "a wide array of views and positions on the global order". 
Trump has also been quite vocal against Brics, particularly its efforts to reduce global trade's dependence on the US dollar, commonly known as de-dollarisation. 
He has often warned the group against trying to come up with an alternative currency or take measures to weaken the dollar's dominance in global trade. 
In one such threat, Trump said in November 2024 that Brics countries would face "100% tariffs" if they backed another currency to replace the "mighty US dollar". 
Under these circumstances, what can the group realistically deliver? 
Brics' geopolitical and economic heft has grown substantially over the past decade. While it will be reluctant to take an openly anti-US or anti-Western position, the group will be looking to build on its existing achievements and demonstrate that it can emerge as an alternative blocs like the G20 and G7. 
Brics now accounts for 49% of the world's population, 40% of global GDP and 26% of international trade, according to BBC Monitoring's analysis. 
Its most tangible achievement remains the New Development Bank - which has approved billions of dollars in infrastructure and development projects - many of them in countries of the global south. 
The group has also created a $100bn contingency reserve arrangement to help members facing financial crises, although it has yet to be tested. 
The leaders are also likely to explore ways to make cross-border payments in local currencies easier. That will be of particular interest to Moscow and Tehran, both of which face severe US sanctions. 
Brics is also expected to continue positioning itself as a voice for the developing nations, collectively pushing for reforms to institutions such as the United Nations, International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, which many developing nations feel do not accurately reflect the new global order. 
For India, in particular, the summit offers an opportunity to strengthen its claim to leadership of the global south. 
Many of Delhi's own foreign policy priorities, including multilateralism, a more multipolar world, greater representation for developing countries and freer global trade, align closely with Brics' wider agenda. 
But India will also have to find ways to work around China's considerable influence within Brics and its stronger presence across much of the developing world. 
The Modi government has placed a strong emphasis on becoming a "leader or a voice of the Global South", Kugelman says. But India's efforts have had "limited success" in making deeper inroads in Africa and Latin America, where China has been more successful. 
With most Brics members coming from developing economies, Kugelman says the expanded grouping gives India an opportunity to deepen ties with countries such as Ethiopia, Brazil and Indonesia and build a stronger profile across Africa and Latin America. 
Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, 
The war in Iran and its economic fallout are expected to be high on the agenda 
For Delhi, the test will be whether it can secure a consensus statement - often seen as a measure of a host nation's diplomatic success. That will be difficult given sharp differences over the Iran war, relations with the US and the future of global trade. 
The scale of the challenge was evident in May, when Brics foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement after their summit because of differences over the Iran war, leaving host India to issue a chair's summary instead. 
India will take confidence from its experience as G20 host in 2023, when it managed to secure a joint declaration despite deep divisions over Russia's war in Ukraine. 
But Delhi will also want substantive announcements and to highlight what Brics has already achieved. On this, members are likely to agree: none will want the grouping dismissed as merely a "talk shop". 
Leaders are expected to explore ways to strengthen financial cooperation and may make substantive announcements. They are also likely to address major geopolitical developments, with any language on the US is expected to be carefully crafted to avoid confrontation. 
Washington, for its part, will be watching closely. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Delhi has been converted into a fortress with thousands of security personnel deployed as leaders start arriving for the weekend summit 
The summit will also provide the setting for several important bilateral meetings. Chinese President Xi Jinping's meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday will be keenly watched. The two countries have been slowly rebuilding ties, although progress has been more cautious than either side might have hoped. 
Modi is also due to meet President Vladimir Putin, with the war in Ukraine likely to feature prominently in their discussions. 
Modi made a highly public appeal for peace when he met Putin last month on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek. While some interpreted his remarks as a rebuke to Moscow, Russia did not see them that way and publicly welcomed Modi's efforts. 
Beyond geopolitics, India's growing trade deficit with both Russia and China is also likely to feature in the bilateral discussions. 
But in the end, the group's focus will be on concluding a successful summit as it would add further weight to Brics' influence. 
And for host India, it would also be a diplomatic and geopolitical achievement at a time when Delhi is seeking to reassert its international influence. 
Kugelman says the stakes are particularly high for India at this summit. 
Delhi, he argues, has been somewhat overshadowed by Pakistan's recent diplomatic role in the Middle East, including its involvement in mediation efforts around the Iran war. 
"This is an important opportunity for India to reassert its global significance and its global leadership," he says. "That is one reason why the stakes are high." 
The summit, he adds, is in some ways "more important for India as host than it is for the Brics grouping as a whole".

articles.title: Hong Kong's Tiananmen activists sentenced to up to seven years in prison
articles.summary: Hong Kong used to be one of the only places in Chinese territory where people could gather to mark the 1989 crackdown.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Speaking to the BBC before her arrest in 2022, Chow said she was "prepared to be arrested" By Koh Ewe   and   BBC Chinese 
- Published 11 September 2026 
Three Hong Kong activists who organised annual vigils commemorating Beijing's 1989 crackdown on Tiananmen Square protests have been handed prison sentences of up to seven years. 
Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and Chow Hang-tung, 41, were convicted last month of inciting others to subvert state power, under the city's controversial national security law. A third defendant, Albert Ho, 74, had pleaded guilty in January. 
The office of United Nations human rights chief Volker Türk called for "these sentences to be quashed". 
Hong Kong and Macau were for years the only places on Chinese soil where people could hold gatherings to mark the Tiananmen crackdown - a highly sensitive and heavily censored topic in mainland China. 
These gatherings were banned by Hong Kong's authorities in 2020, citing Covid-19 policies, but never resumed. That same year, the national security law, which makes illegal a wider range of dissenting acts, officially came into force. 
Authorities say the law is necessary to maintain stability, but critics argue it has eroded Hong Kong's autonomy and created a climate of fear. 
Lee, Chow and Ho were charged in 2021. They faced up to 10 years in prison after their conviction. 
On Friday, the court sentenced Lee to seven years in prison, while Chow was handed seven years and three months. Ho, who pleaded guilty, was sentenced to five years in prison. 
As the court session started, Chow and Lee stood up and smiled at the public gallery, which was full of people. Ho wore a serious expression. 
After their sentences were handed down, Lee appeared to pray as he was led out of the dock, while Chow blew a kiss to those seated in the public gallery. 
According to a court summary in August, Lee and Chow had "incited other persons to organise, plan, commit or participate in acts by unlawful means with a view to subverting the state power". 
Chow told the court in May the law itself was on trial. 
A key part of the trial concerned the group's slogan of "ending one-party dictatorship", which the court said had incited people to undermine the Chinese Communist Party. 
Lee's wife, Elizabeth Tang, told Reuters that it was a "sad day" for her. 
"I cannot imagine that he has to spend another three years in jail, it is really unacceptable," she said, adding that Lee intended to appeal his sentence. 
Chow's mother Medina told a crowd outside the court not to be "overly saddened" about the verdict. "Do not lose heart. And above all, do not feel guilty," she said, Reuters reported. 
Speaking to the BBC before her arrest in 2022, Chow said she was "prepared to be arrested" and "willing to pay the price for fighting for democracy". 
Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images Image caption, 
People in Hong Kong used to hold yearly vigils commemorating Beijing's 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown 
The defendants were leaders of the now-disbanded Hong Kong Alliance, a group founded in May 1989 to support students holding pro-democracy rallies. 
Weeks later, the Chinese Communist Party sent troops and tanks to crush pro-democracy protests in Beijing's Tiananmen Square. Estimates of the death toll range from a few hundred to many thousands. 
Over the next three decades, the Hong Kong Alliance called on authorities to accept responsibility for the crackdown, free dissidents and introduce democratic reform. 
The group also held yearly vigils commemorating the Tiananmen Square crackdown. Organisers said some of the gatherings attracted more than 100,000 people, though police had lower estimates of the turnout. 
On Friday, the court also handed a HK$1.5m fine ($191,000; £142,000) to the Hong Kong Alliance. 
"This sentencing is a triple tragedy: for the activists being unjustly punished; the survivors and victims of the Tiananmen crackdown itself; and the generations of Hongkongers denied the space to discuss one of the most consequential events in modern Chinese history," said Amnesty International's Deputy Regional Director Sarah Brooks. 
"The harsh sentences against peaceful Tiananmen vigil organisers expose the cruelty and insecurity of a government afraid of memory and the people," Human Rights Watch said in a statement.

articles.title: Anthropic boss Dario Amodei calls for AI development to slow down
articles.summary: The call comes amid growing concerns that AI models may become able to inflict serious damage worldwide.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
There was no alternative to developing AI, Anthropic boss Dario Amodei said By Paulin Kola   and   Lily Jamali ,  North America Technology correspondent ,  Reporting from San Francisco 
- Published 12 September 2026, 16:37 BST Updated 2 hours ago 
The head of AI company Anthropic has called for the pace of development of artificial intelligence models to slow down and to be closely monitored. 
In an essay, Dario Amodei said developing AI was not in question, but the risks associated with it were "serious" and companies and governments must be given time to address them. 
The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk, have both said they agree with Amodei. 
There have been growing concerns recently about the technology's potential risks. An AI researcher who left Anthropic this week told the BBC that "if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future". 
Jacob Coxon told Laura Kuenssberg that people working at AI companies were "genuinely frightened... genuinely concerned about the fate of humanity in the next two years". 
"It's not at all an exaggeration to say that the people who are involved with both founding these companies and building the tech believe there is a possibility of human extinction," Coxon said. 
"Many of the people who are sort of deep in the weeds on actually coding the thing believe that there is like a greater than ten percent chance, or even greater. Some smaller, but they all have different numbers for a probability that humans might die. And they all keep this in their head on a daily basis while working on the technology." 
- 
Dramatic insider warnings over AI fall flat with some in Silicon Valley 
- Published 6 hours ago 
In Amodei's essay, called We Must Pace the Frontier and made public on Saturday, he proposed a three-point plan that includes independent monitoring of AI models as they are developed, industry-wide regulation and global regulation. 
As his proposal made the rounds, even competitors voiced support for the idea of third-party monitors who could evaluate the safety of models as they are developed. 
"I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier," wrote OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on X. He called independent evaluators "a great idea." 
In a new interview with Fortune Magazine, Altman had sounded similar safety concerns, saying standards were "not at a place" to push AI capabilities much further. 
He added that he believed AI beyond human control is "absolutely" possible. 
Elon Musk meanwhile said the Anthropic boss was "right". 
The warnings have prompted calls to action, but US President Donald Trump has so far rejected such fears, saying on Thursday he was concerned "if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position". 
Cyber-security concerns have grown as new models have exhibited more and more powerful hacking capabilities. 
Anthropic withheld its Mythos model from public use when it was announced in April that it could independently escape the testing environment, known as the sandbox. 
In the run-up to the release of its most recent Astra model, OpenAI cited cybersecurity concerns as it explained it had paused certain aspects of the model's development. 
Safety has also taken centrestage in the rivalry between Anthropic and OpenAI. 
Amodei, who had previously worked as a vice president at OpenAI, has said he co-founded Anthropic in 2021 so he could build safer and more trusted AI models. 
In his essay, Amodei pointed out that AI had advanced "drastically faster" including its "ability to build the next generation of AI" - and mentioned an incident involving rival OpenAI which has revealed that agents conducted cybersecurity attacks , external on targets they were not asked to attack in July. 
The OpenAI agents had "essentially acted as a fanatically devoted collective", Amodei said. OpenAI has said it is slowing down training of certain advanced AI models and tools as a result. 
Amodei called for "building AI at a balanced rate that aims to ensure its safety while still achieving its benefits". 
This would not mean "halting model training or technical progress, but ensuring companies take adequate time to align and safeguard their models, and for third party evaluators to confirm this". 
He was committing Anthropic to this "unilaterally" - as well as calling on governments "to require other frontier companies to match". 
Amodei said he recognised that regulation might not be able to keep up with the pace of AI, and therefore called on AI companies to "voluntarily work together to set standard" in parallel with regulation. 
The Anthropic CEO went on to address the impact that a slowdown would have on the industry and competition with leading developers worldwide, particularly China. 
"I believe that if slowing down bought us even an extra year or two before models reach critical levels of capability, and we used that time to advance alignment, we could greatly reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong," Amodei said. 
This would have to be done in a co-ordinated manner "without sacrificing commercial advantage or the United States' lead in AI". Any slowdown would have to be limited, he said, to avoid allowing China to pull ahead. 
He urged the US government to take measures so that US companies' AI chips could not be sold to China - or the technology shared with authoritarian countries. 
His former employee, Jacob Coxon, told the BBC, however, that the initiative to slow down must go beyond the US - "there'll need to be some sort of co-ordinated slowdown with China if we're going to avoid a race at an international scale". 
Amodei's post has prompted a wide range of responses. 
Clement Delangue, the CEO of the AI platform Hugging Face, said he was launching a new project called the Open Alignment Initiative, adding he wanted to be among "embedded evaluators" that Amodei proposed could be part of a solution. 
Hugging Face was hacked by OpenAI agents earlier this year prompting an outcry over AI safety. 
"Let's make AI safer by making it more transparent," Delangue wrote on X. 
Elon Musk also voiced his support, writing that "Dario is right". 
Musk, whose SpaceXAI makes the controversial chatbot Grok, once called Anthropic "evil" but has changed his tone since signing a $15bn deal to sell compute capacity to Anthropic in May. 
However some observers suggested that Amodei's post was less about safety than about consolidating control over AI technology. 
"Dario makes the case to stop open source and concentrate enormous technological and economic power with Anthropic," wrote Chamath Palihapitiya, investor and co-host of the tech podcast "All-In". 
Notions of slowing down or even pausing AI development have long been met with such cynicism in certain corners of Silicon Valley, with critics accusing leading AI developers of hyping their technology as a marketing ploy. 
Anthropic and OpenAI are both reportedly preparing for potentially record-setting initial public offerings.

articles.title: Five minutes to steal a Renoir: Why museum thefts are becoming bolder across Europe
articles.summary: Art crime investigators and security experts say burglaries from galleries across Europe are becoming more brazen.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters/Museum Renoir Image caption, 
The latest heist, at the Renoir museum in the south of France, saw thieves break in by cutting through a fence with an electric knife and hacksaw By Mallory Moench 
- Published 12 September 2026, 01:24 BST 
When thieves broke into a French museum earlier this week and stole four paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir, worth millions of euros, not everyone was surprised. 
Just last month, the European policing agency (Europol) had warned that museum thefts across Europe were growing increasingly brazen. 
And just days before the Renoir heist, internationally known art detective Arthur Brand predicted to the BBC that more high-profile burglaries were likely - particularly in the wake of the successful robbery at the Louvre in Paris last October . 
The audacious crime in one of the world's most famous museums stunned France, and the stolen jewellery worth €88m (£75m) has still not been recovered, nearly a year on. 
"We will see more of this," says Brand, "because if you are able to hit the Louvre, thieves all around the world are watching that, thinking, 'Wow' - and then they think, 'Don't we have a local museum with gold and silver?'". 
Figure caption, 
What we know about the Renoir museum heist 
Within hours of the Louvre burglary, thieves had raided coins from a smaller museum in France. Since then, criminals have stolen a diamond necklace in Vienna , Bronze Age artefacts in Spain , and art from two Italian museums - and that's only what the BBC has written about. 
The heist at the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer is the latest, and detectives are still working to track down the remaining multi-million-pound paintings - two of which were quickly recovered after thieves dropped them in the museum garden. 
Europol tells the BBC the number of museum theft cases reported to them across Europe began to increase about two years ago. 
Its recent report says both the methods and targets of thefts are changing - with a rise in more forceful tactics, and, as in the Louvre case, a focus on high-value items such as precious metals and gemstones. 
Both Brand and Ibrahim Bulut, a museum security expert from a Belgian security consulting firm, believe many thefts that followed the Louvre burglary are copycats. 
"Every museum in the world is stressing now," Brand says. "In every museum there have been meetings with the security officer or with the police."

The Association for Research into Crimes against Art (ARCA) says the recent thefts show "a repeated preference for small, portable, immediately accessible objects and for attacks designed to be completed in minutes". 
Data provided to the BBC by ARCA shows recorded museum thefts in France spiked in 2024, and rose again slightly in 2025. 
However, numbers go up and down over time, with more thefts recorded in 2015 than a decade later. 
Image source, Arthur Brand Image caption, 
Art detective Brand helped track down this Vincent van Gogh painting, which was stolen in 2023 and eventually dropped off to him by an unknown man 
These crimes threaten what many consider invaluable artefacts of historical and cultural value enjoyed by the public - although some people argue they steal "from the rich, who cares?" Brand says. 
Others point out the colonial history behind many treasures in European museums, with art historians highlighting the French crown jewels stolen from the Louvre contained emeralds, diamonds, sapphires and pearls which are not native to France. 
Why are museums being targeted? 
Museums are vulnerable and easy to burgle, Brand says, compared with well-secured jewellery shops and banks - which these days hold less cash. 
Directors historically "never have enough money for security" or prefer to spend it on the next exhibition, and museums are often housed in old buildings that are difficult to protect, he adds. 
For example, the Denis Diderot Maison des Lumières (House of Enlightenment) - burgled hours after the Louvre - is housed in two 18th-Century mansions in Langres. 
"We therefore have to reconcile modern security requirements with the need to preserve historic buildings and comply with France's heritage regulations," local mayor Théo Caviezel explains. 
Museums are also open public spaces that have less access control and perpetrators can come in as visitors, says Kumar Sokka, CEO of Acre Security which works with some museums in Europe. 
And even if a museum is secured well, thieves could still come in armed, Brand says, adding that it would be impractical to put police in galleries. 
Many of these burglaries are over in minutes and the thieves have long gone by the time police show up - the Renoir case happened within five minutes. 
Heists used to depend on deception, but burglaries are now becoming increasingly violent, Europol's report last month , external points out. Offenders are using tools such as sledgehammers, axes, crowbars and, in some instances, explosives, to get inside. 
In the Louvre, the thieves used a mechanical lift to gain access, cut through the window with power tools and then threatened guards, who left, before forcing their way inside displays and grabbing the jewels. In the Renoir case, the perpetrators used an electric knife to cut through a fence before sawing through structures holding the paintings' frames in place. 
The increased aggression creates new security concerns. 
"An armed incident during opening hours, like the one we experienced, creates a situation in which the immediate priority is to keep our audience and staff safe," says Lilli Hollein, the director of the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) in Vienna, which was burgled last month. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: Two people leave Louvre in lift mounted to vehicle 
What is being stolen is also changing. While paintings are still taken, they're harder to sell, so about 10 years ago, thieves began shifting to goods that are easier to get rid of, Brand says. 
Now precious metals, gemstones, and culturally significant artefacts including Chinese porcelain are increasingly targeted, according to Europol's report. 
"Precious metals can be easily melted down, leaving no trace for law enforcement, and facilitating illicit sales during the fencing process," it says. "Precious stones in jewellery, on the other hand, can be easily removed and sold further." 
Meanwhile, Chinese porcelain is likely to be easily sold on the art market because of high demand, Europol says. 
After a theft, police generally have between four and six days to catch the thieves, according to Brand, who works with investigators by calling informants and receiving tips from the public or even ex-partners of perpetrators. 
But while suspects may be arrested, jewels or precious metals might not be found - such as with the Louvre case. 
On the other hand, Brand believes the Renoir paintings stolen this week - two of which were dropped by the thieves on their way out - "will probably be recovered" because "no one will want to buy" them and "it is likely, then, that the thieves have no idea what to do with them". 
Christopher A Marinello, the boss of Art Recovery International that recovers stolen art, says only 5-10% of stolen art is ever recovered, making thefts from small museums like this week's "extra painful". 
Tuesday's heist is another example of "Europe's museums under siege", he adds. 
So how can museums be protected? 
After its theft in October, Maison des Lumières launched a security audit carried out by police officers appointed by France's cultural ministry, mayor Caviezel says. 
Some recommendations are already being implemented, such as enhanced video surveillance, while other structural improvements are in the process of being developed. 
MAK in Vienna also increased its security to prevent "copycat offenders and to provide our audience with visible security", its director says. Entry is through a metal detector, and bags must be put in the cloakroom or in lockers, and there are more security guards. 
Experts say the trick is to create physical barriers that will delay thieves so there is time for the police to arrive, or to make any theft take so long that it would deter would-be offenders from attempting it. 
"Security is about buying time", says Bulut. "The objective is not to make the theft theoretically impossible, but to make removal difficult, noisy, detectable and above all, time-consuming, because to be very honest, thefts can always happen, it's the timing that you're concerned about." 
Image source, Jeremy Audouard/AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
The gap at the museum exhibition in Vienna, where a necklace decorated with more than 600 diamonds was on display before thieves smashed the glass and made off with it 
Brand says a delay could be building an extra, heavy door anchored into the ground, thickening the glass on display cases or using a fog machine. 
Sokka says it's critical to have integrated systems - so for example if an alarm goes off, you could shut down the facility, or lock down all high net worth paintings. 
However, security measures are expensive. Mayor Caviezel, whose small French city hosts two museums and collections, says finding the money is "one of our main challenges". 
"A small city can be entrusted with collections of national importance without having the financial resources of a major Parisian institution." 
Bulut, who sits on the International Committee for Museum Security board, says it's not all about expensive gadgets. It could also be training guards to spot suspicious people who may be casing a museum and ask them if they need help, which may deter them from returning. 
Museums are investing: Sokka says his company has seen an uptick in seismic offerings, that can detect vibration such as drilling in walls, in the past 18 months. 
Museum heists are not increasing everywhere in Europe. In Sweden, major museum thefts began to decline around a decade ago and have not changed significantly in recent years, said Peg Magnusson, Sweden's representative for a Unesco convention to combat illicit trafficking of cultural property. However, other worrying cultural artefact targets have emerged. 
The challenge for museums now is increasing security while also staying open to the public. 
"A museum cannot be a fortress," Hollein says. "We want to be open institutions; at the same time, we are facing new challenges and attacks against museums that will require new standards."

Xi Jinping, right, is visiting India for the first time in seven years to attend the Brics summit. Photograph: Indian ministry of foreign affairs/EPA 
View image in fullscreen 
Xi Jinping, right, is visiting India for the first time in seven years to attend the Brics summit. Photograph: Indian ministry of foreign affairs/EPA 
Xi Jinping gets red carpet at Brics summit amid thaw in India-China relations
Chinese president’s arrival in Delhi seen as step towards reconciliation after deadly 2020 military clash 
The Chinese president, Xi Jinping , has received a red-carpet welcome in India for a summit of Brics developing nations, as regional rivals Beijing and Delhi make a public display of thawing relations while quietly competing to lead at a time of shaky US global dominance. 
As Xi stepped off the plane, he was walked past an honour guard of Indian soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses. Later on Saturday, he was due to attend a gala dinner for the two-day summit. 
The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, and Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, had already been welcomed by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi , who is hosting one of the group’s most closely watched gatherings since its inception. 
The summit marks Xi’s first visit to India in seven years and is seen as the biggest step towards reconciliation after a deadly 2020 military clash along the disputed Himalayan border, in which ‌20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers were killed. 
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming recently , with flights and high-level contacts gradually being restored. China was “willing” to work with India to properly manage differences and be “good neighbours and friends”, China’s foreign ministry said on Friday. 
Leaders and diplomats have been convening in India for the annual gathering of the Brics grouping, named after five of its earliest members – Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – that was conceived as a counterweight to western dominance. 
This summit comes as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with rising US-China tensions, test the bloc’s ability to find common ground. 
Since its inception in 2009, Brics has expanded as a forum for major emerging economies to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The group now rivals the US-dominated G7 forum of advanced economies, accounting for half of the global population. 
But its growth has also created new fractures and disunity – Iran was bombing Saudi Arabia and the UAE earlier this year, and Brics foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in Delhi in May. 
On Saturday, the bloc managed to unanimously agree on the wording of a joint declaration that reiterated a commitment to peaceful resolution of international disputes “through dialogue, consultation and diplomacy”. 
The “New Delhi declaration” ​called for “maximum restraint” in the Middle East, although it was worded so as not to call out member countries actively involved in conflicts. 
Jiang Shixue, the vice-president of the expert committee of the China thinktank Council for BRICs cooperation (China), said the 11 members “cannot speak with one voice on many issues”. 
“The only solution is to continuously strengthen political consensus,” he told the South China Morning Post. 
Beijing and Delhi have differing views on the role of the group. 
China has sought to expand Brics power as a counterweight to the US under Donald Trump’s leadership, which has launched global tariff and trade wars and retreated from multilateral institutions such as the UN, which afforded it international credibility. 
India has taken a more cautious approach, seeing Brics as a bridge between the west and the developing world. 
Saturday’s talks began with an address by Modi, who said Brics was “not against anyone”. 
Chietigj Bajpaee, a senior research fellow for South Asia in the Asia-Pacific programme at Chatham House, said this week that Delhi had found it hard to maintain its policy of “strategic hedging” during such a disruptive US presidency. 
“India’s position can appear out of sync in a forum whose membership includes countries with more overtly anti-western agendas, including China, Russia and Iran. And two other Brics countries, South Africa and Brazil, have suffered high-profile diplomatic disputes with the US,” he wrote. 
“The challenge for Delhi is that it wishes to promote this worldview in a way that is non-western but not explicitly anti-western.” 
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

articles.full_text:

View image in fullscreen 
The former Hong Kong Alliance leaders Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung were found guilty of ‘incitement to subversion’ in August. Photograph: Peter Parks/AFP/Getty Images 
Tiananmen Square vigil organisers jailed for seven years in Hong Kong
Pro-democracy activists Chow Hang-tung and Lee Cheuk-yan were found guilty of ‘incitement to subversion’ in controversial national security case 
Two pro-democracy activists who were put on trial for organising an annual Tiananmen Square massacre vigil in Hong Kong have been sentenced to seven years in jail, in one of the city’s most significant national security cases. 
Chow Hang-tung, 41 and Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, were found guilty in August of incitement to subversion . The court found they had “incited other persons to organise, plan, commit or participate in acts by unlawful means with a view to subverting the state power”. 
Chow and Lee were leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance, which for decades organised the city’s annual vigil in memory of those killed in the bloody crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in Beijing in 1989. Lee and Chow received prison terms of seven years, and seven years and three months respectively. 
Albert Ho, a 74-year-old former lawmaker who pleaded guilty in January, received a sentence of five years and two months. 
Their case represented one of the last high-profile national security trials to be heard in Hong Kong, as the national security law imposed by Beijing in 2020 extinguishes what was once one of the world’s most widely watched pro-democracy struggles. The Alliance disbanded in 2021 following pressure created by the introduction of the national security law. ‘She’s not afraid of anyone’: the prison writings of one of Hong Kong’s last outspoken democracy activists 
Read more 
The case had centred on a slogan that was used for decades by the Alliance: “end one-party dictatorship”. The court ruled that the defendants “intended to cause others to lose confidence in the Chinese Communist party by stirring up hostility and causing division”. The defence said that the Alliance was simply exercising its right to freedom of speech. 
One supporter who attended the sentencing told the Guardian: “A demonstration that lasted for more than 35 years without any problem is suddenly being seen as subversion.” 
Chow, a UK educated barrister, represented herself in court. She has been in detention since 2021 and while in prison has frequently written letters published on her social media. 
In August Chow wrote a note to the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, calling for Britain “to adopt a more robust stance in the face of the growing threat from a totalitarian and aggressive China”. The UK Foreign Office said it condemned the use of the national security law in convicting the two activists. 
Before sentencing, members of the public queued up for days to secure a seat in the court. Some in the queue had prepared food and umbrellas in preparation to stay overnight. 
Hong Kong and Macau were once the only places on Chinese soil where it was permitted to hold public vigils to mourn protesters who died on 4 June 1989 in Beijing. Hundreds, possibly thousands, were killed when the People’s Liberation Army put a bloody end to pro-democracy protests . 
View image in fullscreen 
Elizabeth Tang Yin-ngor, wife of former Hong Kong Alliance leader Lee Cheuk-yan, leaves West Kowloon magistrates courts on 21 August. Photograph: Tyrone Siu/Reuters 
For decades tens of thousands of people would gather in Hong Kong’s Victoria park to take part in a candlelit vigil. In 2020, Beijing’s sweeping national security law in effect banned public commemoration. In recent years, activists who attempted to publicly mark the day said they were frequently followed, searched and detained by plainclothes police. 
Authorities said the national security law would only affect a small number of people and was needed to return order after a year of often violent anti-government protests in 2019. But critics say it has transformed the city. 
“It is still surreal to me,” Lee’s wife, Elizabeth Tang, told the Guardian. “Every time the Alliance had an activity, they would get the police permission for every one. 
“The vigils are what made Hong Kong different,” she said, recalling the public commemoration that are now banned. “It’s very unjust. Complete silence is really very scary.” 
The case has seen widespread condemnation from foreign governments and human rights groups who criticised the use of the national security law to convict peaceful protesters and ban the vigil.
